Conclusions The study has established the suitability of Bambusa spinosa as a prime candidate for fabricating glue-laminated bamboo (GLB) beams, particularly using culms harvested in Cagayan de Oro, Philippines. The species exhibited mechanical properties that surpass the minimum strength requirements for structural GLB applications. Optimal culms were identified as those with a diameter of 40–50 mm and a wall thickness of 5–7 mm, ideally harvested 3 m above the base and aged 3–4 years. A treatment process involving a 7-day salt solution immersion significantly enhanced the mechanical properties of the bamboo while preventing infestations by damaging agents such as fungi. For fabrica- tion, phenol-formaldehyde adhesive was employed under a pressing pressure of 2 MPa to ensure uniform bonding. GLB samples tested were sized at 50 mm × 100 mm × 800 mm and 50 mm × 125 mm × 800 mm, achieving structural integrity and consistency in properties. Conclusions We have proposed a new methodology for using bamboo as a structural element. Bamboo slat structural beams are more than an interesting material; they represent a significant shift toward sustainability. Structural beams made of slatted bamboo derived from Dendrocalamus asper exhibited the best performance in the bending tests, both in terms of maximum load capacity and deflection. For an applied load of approximately 16 kN, the specimens presented a deflection of about 80 mm. A comparison of the tested specimens highlighted the importance of reinforcement through the use of threaded rods, which improved the confinement of the bamboo slats and consequently enhanced the me- chanical performance of the structural element. It was not possible to establish a direct correlation between the fibre volume and the me- chanical properties of the structural element. Despite achieving superior results in tensile tests, Phyllostachys edulis showed the lowest performance in bending tests, reaching a deflection of approximately 80 mm under a load of 14 kN. Conclusions and future scope With the diminishing supply of high-quality timber resources, en- terprises and researchers have been obliged to search for and use nat- ural lignocellulosic materials such as bamboo. Bamboo resources are widely distributed and are considered an eco-friendly alternative to commonly used timber species. The utilization of bamboo in its round form presents several challenges due to its irregular shape and large variability in properties. Some of these issues can be overcome through the structural grading of round bamboo culms or by transforming the round bamboo culms into relatively regular cross-sectional composites. Researchers have developed several structural bamboo composites that provide a material with uniform cross sections, improving the utilisa- tion potential of bamboo. LBL and SBL are two SBCs that have recently emerged as possible substitutes for conventional construction materials because they are environmentally friendly and have competitive phy- sical and mechanical properties.
